title: Application Entry & Shell
description: Start here: CornerCV6 is the root component /dashboard renders, a view-machine router that mounts every screen (Home, Chat, Support, Command, Tracker, LiveScribe, Search) and fans out to 25 internal modules. Around it sits the persistent shell you see on every screen: SharedNav is the one canonical navigation (desktop tool bar plus mobile drawer reading the same ordered NAV_TOOLS list), and ActivityDock floats live Claude agent sessions across the surface. Understanding this file tells you how a screen is selected and how the whole app is wired together.
languageLesson: CV6 composes screens by filling Claude Design HTML templates imported with Vite's ?raw suffix through a TemplateScreen helper, rather than hand-drawing JSX. A view-machine router is just a state variable naming the active screen plus a switch that renders it — the same pattern React apps use before reaching for a routing library.

title: The Shared Data Spine
description: Every screen gets real data from one place. DataContext wraps a single useDataPipe at the top level and a single CommandProvider, collapsing 6+ redundant polling loops and Supabase subscriptions into one shared source. The use* hooks are the view-models that shape that raw feed for each screen: useHomeData builds the Home agents/projects/Catch-Up view and creation helpers, while useCommandTracker feeds the live activity dock and the 24h room ledger. Learn this layer and you understand how the whole surface stays consistent and avoids fabricated data.
languageLesson: React Context lets one provider high in the tree expose data to any descendant without prop-drilling. Here it doubles as a de-duplication layer: one subscription in the provider replaces many identical fetches scattered across components, so screens read from context instead of each opening their own polling loop.

title: Seed & UI-Contract Data
description: Because screens are filled templates, each one has a JSON data-binding contract that declares the shape the template expects — regions, field names, actions, states, and responsive modifiers. chat.json defines the goal-thread vocabulary, home-desktop.json is shaped to the useHomeData hook from Step 2, and command.json and tracker.json describe the Command and bug-Tracker screens. kit.json is the shared agent-chat element vocabulary (turn, message, block templates) cloned across Chat, Support, Command, and Live Scribe. These files are the contract between the hooks that produce data and the templates that render it.
languageLesson: This is contract-driven UI: the JSON is a schema that names every field, action, and state a screen needs, so the data hook and the HTML template can be built and changed independently as long as both honor the contract.

title: Chat Orchestration
description: Chat is the richest feature, and two orchestrators assemble it. ChatDesktop is the three-pane desktop surface (room/project navigation, a files shelf, and the message thread) with agent-control actions like handoff, pause, and retask. ChatLifecycle is the mobile/lifecycle counterpart that stitches together day-grouped messages, goal turns, file galleries, dictation, and the composer by pulling renderers from the other chat modules. Both are fed by useRoomThread, which turns one room's real Supabase messages into the oldest-to-newest Turn contract the chat surface renders.

title: Message & Block Rendering
description: This is the engine behind every chat message. MessageThread groups messages by sender and renders desktop and mobile turns, attaching goal-thread bodies, result blocks, attachments, and link cards. BlockRenderer is the structured-block library — a Result dispatcher plus one component per agent block type (email, summary, artifact, data table, code diff, gallery, question, confirm). ChatGoalThread turns agent blocks and live steps into a work timeline of step rows, work-done cards, and proposals, and ResultLinkCard renders link-preview rows. blockSchema.js defines the BLOCK_TYPES catalog and factory helpers that all of this rendering keys off of.
languageLesson: BlockRenderer is a tagged-union dispatcher: each message block carries a type field, and a single Result component switches on that type to pick the matching renderer. Adding a new agent output type means adding one entry to the blockSchema catalog and one case to the dispatcher — the rest of the pipeline stays untouched.

title: Composers & Attachments
description: How a user actually sends input. Cv6FullComposer is the portal-mounted input experience with attachments, recording, voice mode, and slash commands, wrapped in an error boundary with read-only and mini fallbacks. Cv6InputBar is the leaner input bar with slash-command autocomplete, image and integrations pickers, and paste-chip handling. NewComposer is the single start-a-mission / new-project overlay opened from Home and Organize on both breakpoints, and MessageAttachments renders inbound images, galleries with a lightbox, and file collections with download/review actions. Together they close the loop from the rendering pipeline in Step 5 back to user action.

title: Document & Media Viewers
description: These small helper modules are the most widely depended-upon files in the codebase — the Organize and Review screens both lean on them to preview whatever a user or agent produced. docxDocView, htmlDocView, and pdfDocView each expose a use*Docs hook that hydrates and previews their file type in the viewer shell, with htmlDocView carefully rewriting relative asset and CSS URLs for safe in-viewer rendering. mediaFallback installs one global media-error handler that swaps any failed video/audio/image for a retry card. Learn these before the screens that consume them.

title: The Responsive Triad: Organize
description: Organize is the clearest example of the pattern every screen follows. Organize.jsx is a thin viewport router that mounts OrganizeDesktop or OrganizeMobile from a max-width:899px media query and forwards props. Both layouts bind the same useOrganize hook — which reads the project_files disk-mirror metadata and lazily previews content using the viewers from Step 7 — so desktop and mobile share one data source but diverge only in presentation. TreeContextMenu is the shared right-click / long-press menu (rename, move, archive, create) reused here, on Home, and in Review. Once you see this triad, you can read every other screen.
languageLesson: The router → Desktop + Mobile triad is CV6's responsive idiom: a media query in the router component decides which layout mounts, so the two variants stay fully separate components rather than one component littered with breakpoint branches, while a single data hook keeps their behavior identical.

title: Review & Pin Comments
description: Review is the deliverables approval feature, and it reuses everything so far. Review.jsx (compact) and ReviewDesktop.jsx both bind useReview, which loads the real deliverables queue from the review-queue API, renders each body with the Step 7 viewers, and wires approve / request-changes as real decision events. ReviewPins provides the pin-comment UI and popover for placing point comments on docs, images, and video frames, and ReviewChanges compiles a reviewer's comments and pins into a single change list sent back to the agent. This is the human-in-the-loop gate where agent output gets accepted or bounced back.

title: Onboarding Flow
description: The guided first-run flow shows the Step 8 triad applied to a stateful wizard. Onboarding.jsx routes to OnboardingDesktop or OnboardingMobile by viewport, and both compose the wired HTML template with loading / error / empty states through TemplateScreen. useOnboarding is the state machine behind it: it tracks auth, the current step index, and theme, and shapes the step / connection / agent / theme view model that both screens consume as the user walks from connecting sources to setting their first goal.

title: Settings Screen
description: Settings reinforces the now-familiar pattern one more time. Settings.jsx routes by media-query breakpoint to SettingsDesktop or a two-view list/detail SettingsMobile, and both compose the static HTML shell with live data from useSettings, which loads the authenticated user, projects, and theme and derives the settings view model. Seeing the same router → Desktop + Mobile + one hook shape a third time confirms it is the project's universal screen contract, not a one-off.

title: Feature Screens: Support, Campaign, LiveScribe & Search
description: These are the specialized tools that round out the surface. SupportDesktop is the Open/Waiting inbox plus email-review pane (AI summary, original email, suggested actions, reply composer) with SupportThread rendering the real Gmail chain behind each ask. Campaign is the cold-outreach mission-control dashboard with a multi-step creation wizard. LiveScribe is the meeting-capture tool that records 15-second audio chunks and transcribes them via Gemini. Search is a client-side command-K palette built in React (not a template) because it is input-driven, filtering Rooms and Missions from the same hooks Home and Chat use.

title: Styling & Design Templates
description: End with the design reference that everything renders against. cv6.css is the single-import stylesheet holding the CV6 token system (color scales, semantic surface/text/accent variables, radii, fonts), frame layout, every screen-primitive class, and the dark, light, and glass themes. The templates/*.html files are the static design mockups — one per screen — that document the intended visual design and are wired once by the screen components you toured above; organize.html, review.html, and chat.html map directly to Steps 8, 9, and 4, while kit.html is the shared agent-chat element vocabulary behind kit.json. This is where you look to judge whether a screen renders the way it was designed to.
languageLesson: CV6 theming is pure CSS custom properties: semantic tokens like surface and accent are defined once on the root and overridden per theme via a data attribute, so switching between dark, light, and glass reassigns variables rather than restyling components. The HTML templates are design-time artifacts, not runtime code — the JSX screens import them and fill in the data.
